allies.rationale_text: First-principles-thinking helps circle-of-control decompose constraints into assumptions and testable actions instead of treating the whole situation as one helpless block.
allies.source_quote: Circle of Control works well with First Principles Thinking, where constraints are decomposed into controllable assumptions and testable actions.
allies.affinity_rationale: Complement — 'works well with First Principles Thinking, where constraints are decomposed into controllable assumptions and testable actions' — useful pairing but 'works well with' indicates moderate complement rather than deep dependency.
allies.activation_condition: When items classified as uncontrollable need to be decomposed into underlying assumptions to test whether some component is actually within the team's influence

allies.rationale_text: Risk-vs-uncertainty helps circle-of-control distinguish what should be hedged from what can actually be changed.
allies.source_quote: It also complements Risk vs. Uncertainty by distinguishing what should be hedged versus what can be actively changed.
allies.affinity_rationale: Complement — 'complements Risk vs. Uncertainty by distinguishing what should be hedged versus what can be actively changed' — helps calibrate the circle boundaries but uses complement language indicating moderate partnership.
allies.activation_condition: When the team needs to distinguish between factors that should be hedged against versus factors where direct action can change the outcome

antagonists.rationale_text: Status-quo-bias undermines circle-of-control by causing teams to classify difficult-but-influenceable factors as 'outside control' without testing whether influence could actually be increased, turning the model into avoidance disguised as realism.
antagonists.source_quote: A common anti-pattern is labeling difficult-but-influenceable factors as 'outside control' too early, which can become avoidance disguised as realism.
antagonists.affinity_rationale: Directly corrupts the model's core function — 'labeling difficult-but-influenceable factors as outside control too early, which can become avoidance disguised as realism' — turns the control classification exercise into a tool for avoiding difficult action.
antagonists.activation_condition: When the team is classifying difficult-but-influenceable factors as uncontrollable without testing whether influence could actually be increased through effort, changed incentives, or new information

structured_tensions.tension_text: Circle-of-control conflicts with systems-thinking when local optimization inside the control circle obscures broader feedback loops.
structured_tensions.source_quote: Potential tension appears with Systems Thinking when local optimization inside the control circle obscures broader feedback loops.

structured_tensions.tension_text: Circle-of-control conflicts with game-theory-payoffs when opponents can shift what is influenceable faster than the current control map assumes.
structured_tensions.source_quote: Another tension appears with Game Theory when opponents can shift your controllable set dynamically.
